To maximize the effect of a recession for restrictive esotropia, one should choose the most restricted muscle (in this case the right medial rectus). Finally just a few high yield tips for TAO questions on standardized tests. Patients can have TAO with any type of thyroid function (hyperthyroid, hypothyroid, or euthyroid). TAO patients should undergo orbital decompression before strabismus surgery before eyelid surgery. TAO patients should not be considered for strabismus surgery until they are out of the active phase of the disease and their alignment measurements are stable. There is no consensus for exactly how long measurements must be stable before considering strabismus surgery but 6-9 months of stability is a good general rule. For standardized testing purposes, never perform a resection for TAO strabismus. In case you have forgotten how to read a strabismus alignment grid, please see the teaching diagram below. For those who may not be familiar, ET stands for esotropia, E for esophoria (patient fusing strabismus), and E(T) means intermittent esotropia (or intermittent fusion and intermittent manifest strabismus).

question: A 26-year old woman presents with significant proptosis, upper eyelid retraction, and diplopia from Graves disease. Which of the following represents the correct order of surgical interventions (if needed) by thyroid eye disease patients?

options.A: orbital decompression, lid surgery, strabismus surgery
options.B: lid surgery, strabismus surgery, orbital decompression
options.C: orbital decompression, strabismus surgery, lid surgery
options.D: strabismus surgery, lid surgery, orbital decompression

explanation: Ocular motility may change significantly after orbital decompression surgery. Therefore, strabismus surgery should only be undertaken *after* orbital decompression surgery (if decompression will be needed). Likewise, upper eyelid retraction may improve or resolve completely after strabismus surgery. Therefore, lid surgery should be postponed until after any significant strabismus is managed.

question: A 35-year-old man presents after head trauma with new-onset diplopia. On examination, you note a left hypertropia that is worse on right gaze and left head tilt. You measure the hypertropia on primary gaze as 10 prism diopters. There is not a significant torsional component on double maddox rod testing. Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial surgery for this patient's condition?
explanation: This patient's clinical presentation is most consistent with a left CN IV palsy. The indications for surgical correction are: diplopia, persistent head tilt, asthenopia, and/or a significant vertical deviation. The surgical management depends on the amount of hypertropia on primary position. If the vertical deviation is 15 prism diopters or less, then ipsilateral inferior oblique weakening is the procedure of choice. If the deviation is more than 15 prism diopters, then recession of the contralateral inferior rectus + ipsilateral inferior oblique weakening is the usual procedure of choice. An alternative for larger hyperdeviations is tucking of the superior oblique tendon if significant tendon laxity is found. Lastly, ipsilateral superior rectus recession is often performed at the same time in both scenarios if forced duction testing shows limited depression on the side of the hypertropia. Comments: IO recession has the benefit of being able to titrate the weakening based on degree of inferior oblique overaction. For 1+ or 2+ overaction, the inferior oblique muscle is recessed 10 mm for 3+ overaction, 12 mm; and 4+ overaction, 14 mm, which is the maximum recession. The muscle is recessed 10 mm by placing the anterior suture 6 mm posterior to the lateral border of the inferior rectus muscle insertion and 4 mm temporal to the lateral border of the inferior rectus. IO recession is a type of IO weakening, other types of weakening include IO myectomy, IO anterior transposition.

question: A mother brings in her 3-year old child with complaints of intermittent inward crossing of both eyes. You write down in your chart: " 30 PD ET and 45 PD ET' ". The cycloplegic refraction shows +2.25 D sphere OD and +2.75 D OS. You initially prescribe the full cycloplegic refraction in a single distance lens which results in orthotropia at distance. However, you still measure 15 PD ET' when the child wears these new glasses. Which of the following pictures shows the correct glasses that should be prescribed for this child?
explanation: This child has an esotropia which is greater at near than at distance. He also has a moderate amount of hyperopia in both eyes. This situation is typical of non-refractive accommodative esotropia where there exists a high AC/A ("accommodative convergence to accommodation") ratio. In addition, the esotropia at near persists despite the child wearing the full cycloplegic refraction. The usual treatment for this condition is the prescription of bifocal glasses, where the bifocal segment is either a +2.50 or +3.00 add. In addition, the bifocal segment should be of the "executive" type where the line bisects the pupil. Lastly, the vertical height of the bifocal segment should not exceed that of the distance segment. Comments: Many practitioners don't really measure the AC/A ratio ever using tests, but use a rule of thumb that if near is more than 10-15 diopters more than distance, the esotropia is high AC/A

question: A 25-year old man presents with the complaints of "sleepy eyes." He also states that it is difficult for him to keep track of objects passing by him while he drives. He started having these symptoms when he was 16-years old, but they have gotten slowly worse over the years. On exam, you shake hands with him without noticing any abnormalities. His fundus exam shows a "lightly-speckled" pigmentary retinopathy OU. Which of the following ancillary tests should this patient undergo?
explanation: This patient demonstrates the classic clinical findings of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO), retinal pigmentary changes, and ptosis. Syndromes that present with CPEO symptoms include Kearns-Sayre syndrome, oculopharyngeal dystrophy, and myotonic dystrophy. CPEO by itself does not have pigmentary retinopathy. I t has progressive ptosis and ophthalmoplegia. It is a mitochondrial disorder and has a mtDNA point deletion. By the 2nd decade of life, symptoms are evident. The systemic symptoms are generalized muscle weakness and muscle biopsy shows "ragged red fibers". In Kearns-Sayre syndrome, patient has CPEO, as well as pigmentary retinopathy. K-S syndrome is also an inherited mitochondrial disease. Cardiac evaluation is essential to rule out heart block as cardiomyopathy and cardiac conduction abnormalities are associated with this condition. Myotonic dystrophy produces symptoms similar to CPEO. In myotonic dystrophy, symptoms are worsened by cold, excitement, and fatigue. It is characteristic for the patient to be unable to let go of his or her grasp when shaking hands or turning a door knob. Myopathic facies ("hatchet face"- wasting of the temporalis and master muscle), frontal balding, and ptosis are often observed. Ocular findings include pigmentary retinopathy, "Christmas tree" cataracts (polychromatic lenticular deposits), ptosis, miotic and sluggish pupils, and ophthalmoparesis. EMG provides diagnosis by showing typical myotonic discharges. In oculopharyngeal dystrophy, the presentation is later in life, around 5th to 6th decade of life. It is an autosomal dominant inherited disease. Presentation is progressive dysphagia followed by muscle weakness, ptosis, and CPEO symptoms. This disease is seen in patients of French-Canadian ancestry.

question: A 6-month old baby presents to your office and the parents state that his eyes have been “crossed” since he was 3-months old. On examination, a large angle esotropia of 50 prism diopters is measured. The patient’s refraction is found to be +1.00 sphere OU. The patient uses both eyes equally (i.e. no apparent amblyopia). What is the next best step in management?

options.A: Surgery to correct the large angle esotropia
options.B: Observation until 2 years of age; since this condition may spontaneously improve by age 2.
options.D: A prescription for the +1.00 with a prism ground into the glasses to correct for

explanation: Most pediatric ophthalmologist agree that surgery to correct the large angle esotropia should be done early; as early as 4 to 6 months of age in a healthy baby. Early surgery maximizes binocular function (stereopsis). Patients who present between the ages of 2-6 months with large angle esotropias are unlikely to improve spontaneously. Prism glasses and alternate patching are not the best treatment option for treatment of infantile esotropia. The treatment is surgery to align the eyes as close to orthotropia as possible. This will allow the development of some degree of sensory fusion.

question: A 45-year-old high myope with a history of scleral buckling surgery in the right eye presents to your office with complaints of double vision since the retinal detachment repair 2 years ago. You note significant restriction of the right medial rectus and wish to perform recession of this muscle. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.A: medial rectus recession via "hang back" technique
options.B: medial rectus recession after removal of the scleral buckle
options.C: medial rectus recession with superior displacement away from the scleral buckle
options.D: medial rectus recession with permanent attachment to the scleral buckle

explanation: Strabismus surgery in the presence of a scleral buckle presents a unique and sometimes challenging situation. In these cases, a "hang back" recession technique can be used whereby the muscle is suspended to the stump of the original insertion with a nonabsorbable suture. This technique is also useful for patients with thin sclera (e.g. high myopes) where a posterior suture pass risks perforation.

question: A 33-year old Caucasian woman presents with a history of ataxia, incontinence, and "weird eye movements." On examination, you note slow adduction of the right eye. Which of the following is true regarding this woman's eye condition?

options.A: the lesion responsible is located on the left side of her brain
options.B: the right eye will fail to adduct on convergence
options.C: esotropia usually occurs due to eventual medial rectus fibrosis
options.D: the abducting eye exhibits a horizontal nystagmus

explanation: This woman has internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) as part of her multiple sclerosis. In this condition, the responsible lesion is *ipsilateral* to the poorly-adducting eye. INO is caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasiculus. There will be normal adduction of the involved eye on convergence.

question: You have just finished performing bilateral medial rectus recessions for a 2-year-old child with congenital esotropia. In the post-operative recovery room, the child appears to be nauseous. Which of the following antiemetic medications is contraindicated for this child?
explanation: Though the topic of using antiemetics in children is somewhat controversial, most experts would NOT use promethazine (brand name: Phenergan) in children 2 years or younger (and with extreme caution in older children). Promethazine can result in severe respiratory depression and even death in this vulnerable population. This serious side effect caused the FDA in 2004 to issue a "boxed warning" contraindicating the medication for children less than 2 years old.

question: A 42-year-old woman presents with binocular double vision for the past few weeks. Her external photograph is shown above. Which of the following extraocular muscles most likely would be affected in this patient's condition?
explanation: This patient has thyroid eye disease until proven otherwise. The hallmark clinical feature of thyroid eye disease is upper eyelid retraction as seen in this photograph. Thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of binocular diplopia in adults. The extraocular muscles affected, in decreasing order of frequency and severity are: inferior rectus, medial rectus, superior rectus, and lateral rectus. Comments: A helpful mnemonic to remember order of muscles affected: "I am slow" = IM SLow, which corresponds to Inferior Medial Superior Lateral.

question: In general, for an incomitant horizontal strabismus caused by a weak muscle with mild residual function, which of the following procedures would most strabismus surgeons choose as an initial procedure?

options.A: resection (strengthening) of the weak muscle alone
options.B: transposition to the adjacent vertical muscles
options.C: weakening of the direct antagonist muscle
options.D: corresponding weakening procedure on the contralateral eye

explanation: In the case of horizontal paralytic incomitant strabismus, one would first grade the amount of weakness of the muscle. If there is a complete paralysis, then one can do a transposition as the first procedure. However, if there is some residual function, most surgeons would use a combination of resection of the weak muscle and recession of the antagonist muscle. In this question, given that the weak muscle has mild residual function, and one can only choose one procedure, strengthening the weak muscle alone will not work as well as weakening the antagonist muscle. A resection will not increase the function of the paralyzed muscle, but will cause restriction (almost like a tether) of the resected muscle; while one can balance the weak muscle and still maintain motility by weakening its antagonist muscle.

question: You are contemplating strabismus surgery in a 1-year old patient with esotropia. The patient already has developed cross-fixation in both eyes. You measure the deviation at distance and near to be 15 prism diopters. Which of the following represents the average amount of recession you should perform in each eye for this patient?
explanation: A table listing the amount of bilateral recessions for an esotropia can be found in standard reference texts (as shown here). In general, one would perform 3.0 mm of recessions on both medial rectus muscles (3 mm on the right, & 3 mm on the left) for 15 prism diopters of esotropia; 4.0 mm for 25 prism diopters; & 5.0 mm for 35 prism diopters. It is important to understand the concept behind strabismus surgery in that a small esotropia of 15 prism diopters needs 3 mm of bilateral medial rectus recession, while a large esotropia of 40 prism diopters will need >5 mm of bilateral medial rectus recession, without referring to a chart. Comments: Easy way to remember: 3 mm x 5 = 15 PD, 4 mm x 6 = 24 (25) PD, 5 mm x 7 = 35 PD. Multiply by successively increasing integers starting from 5.

question: All of the following distinguish cranial nerve (CN) VI palsy from Duane's syndrome EXCEPT:

options.A: absence of upshoots or downshoots in CN VI palsy
options.B: no globe retraction on adduction in CN VI palsy
options.C: lack of significant esotropia in primary position in CN VI palsy
options.D: absence of lid fissure narrowing on attempted adduction in CN VI palsy

explanation: In CN VI palsy, there should be significant esotropia in primary position that is proportional to the severe limitation of abduction seen in this disorder. In contrast, patients with Duane's syndrome typically have only a small-angle (if any) esotropia in primary position.

question: A 5-year-old is brought in by her mother for a "strangely-moving" left eye since birth. On sensorimotor exam, you note the absence of abduction of the left eye, a left face turn, and globe retraction on attempted adduction of the left eye. The rest of her ocular exam is normal. She has no significant family or birth history. The mother is insistent that the child undergo a MRI of the brain to exclude a tumor. Which of the following abnormalities would a MRI of the brain most likely find?

options.A: Fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve
options.B: Slit-like ventricles and partially empty sella turcica
options.D: Hypoplastic or absent nucleus of the sixth cranial nerve

explanation: This patient has Duane retraction syndrome (Type 1), an ocular motility disorder characterized by co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscle leading to horizontal duction deficits and globe retraction on adduction. Globe retraction causes narrowing of the palpebral fissure. The majority of cases are unilateral and involve the left eye (72%). This condition is more common in females. The condition is caused by a hypoplastic sixth nerve nucleus or nerve with aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by the oculomotor nerve. If a patient presents with the classic clinical findings of Duane syndrome, most clinicians would not obtain neuroimaging. An upshoot or downshoot on adduction of the affected eye is sometimes present due to vertical slippage of a tight lateral rectus muscle. The condition is mainly sporadic, followed by autosomal dominant inheritance in 10– 15% of cases. Though typically an isolated abnormality, some patients have associated systemic syndromes such as Goldenhar syndrome (hemifacial microsomia, ocular dermoids, eyelid colobomas) and Wildervanck syndrome (sensorineural hearing loss and Klippel-Feil anomaly). There are three types of Duane syndrome: Type 1: limited abduction Type 2: limited adduction Type 3: limited adduction and abduction There is also something called "synergistic divergence" which is sometimes classified as a fourth type of Duane syndrome. In this very rare condition, there is exotropia and the affected eye actually abducts even further on attempted adduction ("the ocular splits"). Type 1 is the most common, and parents may confuse the deficit as the normal eye turning in, rather than an abduction deficit. As a primary dysinnervation strabismus, surgical management will not normalize eye ductions and surgery is reserved for patients who exhibit a primary position deviation, an abnormal compensatory head posture, significant globe retraction, or large up/downshoots. The majority of patients have the ability for binocular vision, and the goal of any surgery would be to allow for binocularity in primary gaze. WRONG ANSWERS: Choice A: fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve is a classic imaging finding of optic nerve glioma. Choice B: Slit-like ventricles and partially empty sella turcica are common findings in elevated intracranial pressure (e.g. idiopathic intracranial hypertension). Patients with elevated intracranial hypertension can present with sixth nerve palsy. However, these patients would not have globe retraction on attempted adduction. These patients would also be expected to have optic disc edema. Choice C: Lateral rectus aplasia would also not cause globe retraction on adduction.

question: A patient presents with a large angle exotropia. The deviation freely alternates between the two eyes. This deviation is measured to be 40 XT at distance and at near. Surgery is planned based on two consecutive office measurements. Which of the following surgical plans best corrects this patient’s deviation?

options.A: Bilateral lateral rectus recession of 5 mm
options.B: Bilateral medial rectus resection of 5 mm
options.C: Bilateral lateral rectus recession of 8 mm

explanation: It is a good idea to be familiar with basic strabismus surgery numbers for virgin horizontal muscles. For a medium-large angle deviation of 40 prism diopters, the proper amount of surgery to correct the deviation is 8 mm of lateral rectus recession in both eyes. Most strabismus surgeons do symmetrical bilateral recessions instead of bilateral resections. This is mainly due to the fact that most patients experience less pain with a recession. Generally, with any deviation greater than 25 prism diopters, two muscles are operated on as opposed to just one muscle. In this particular case, a bilateral lateral rectus recession of 8 mm can be performed OR a unilateral lateral rectus recession of about 8 mm and a unilateral medial rectus resection of 7 mm on the same eye. I generally perform a 1 muscle surgery for a deviation up to 20 prism diopters, and for any deviation greater than 20 or 25 prism diopters, I perform symmetrical bilateral surgery. Here is a general thought process of how to remember (or guess on an exam) these correction values for recessions: Bilateral ET surgery begins with a bilateral medial rectus (BMR) recession of 3 mm. Bilateral XT surgery begins with a bilateral lateral rectus (BLR) recession of 4 mm. The maximum BMR recession is 6 mm. The maximum BLR recession is 9 mm. Next, try to group categories of deviations as: small (15-25 PD), medium (30- 40 PD), or large (>50 PD) For this patient, he has a "medium/high" deviation and thus requires almost a maximum BLR recession of 9 mm. The closest answer choice to this maximum value is 8 mm. Here is a general thought process of how to remember (or guess on an exam) these correction values for resections: For ET, the resection number is larger than the recession number by ~1 mm. For example, if the deviation was ET 24, then you would recess by 4 mm OR resect by 5 mm. For XT, the resection number is smaller than the recession number by ~2 mm. For example, if the deviation was XT 25, then you would recess by 6 mm OR resect by 4 mm.

question: Which of the following represents the typical first follow-up time period after initiation of full-time patching for amblyopia for a 4-year old child?
explanation: The general rule that is followed to determine the follow-up interval is 1-week per year of age. Therefore, a 4-year old child should be seen again in 4 weeks. Comments: BCSC: "The first follow-up visit after initiation of treatment should occur within 1 week for an infant and after an interval corresponding to 1 week per year of age for the older child (eg, 4 weeks for a 4-year-old).

question: Which of the following tests can quantify the amount of heterotropia a strabismic patient has?

options.C: alternate cover test (prism and cover test)

explanation: The cover-uncover test can only show that a heterotropia is present (i.e. it does not quantify it). The alternate cover and prism test quantifies the TOTAL amount of deviation (i.e. heterotropia + heterophoria). The Hirschberg test is a qualitative test utilizing the corneal light reflex that gives a rough idea of what type of deviation may be present. The simultaneous prism and cover test quantifies only the manifest deviation (i.e. the heterotropia). It is performed by placing a prism in front of the deviating eye and covering the non-deviating (fixating) eye simultaneously. Increasing prism powers are placed until the deviating eye no longer shifts as the fixating eye is covered.

question: A patient presents with a visually-significant right hypertropia of 30 PD. You decide to perform one-muscle surgery to correct this vertical deviation with a right superior rectus recession. What type of eyelid change might occur with this surgery?

options.D: no changes in the upper lid

explanation: Changes in eyelid position almost always occurs with vertical rectus muscle surgery, but more so with inferior rectus than superior rectus muscles. This is due to the connections of the lid retractors with these rectus muscles, both in the upper eyelid and even more so in the lower eyelid. When one performs a resection, one advances the muscle forward, and hence brings along the lid. So for an inferior rectus resection, the lower eyelid will be advanced upwards leading to less inferior scleral show. For a superior rectus resection, the upper eyelid will be advanced downward creating a ptosis-like appearance. Similarly, when one performs a recession, one is moving the rectus muscle further away from the insertion and also moving the eyelid with this recession. So for an inferior rectus recession, the lower eyelid will be pushed away exposing sclera below the lower limbus. For a superior rectus recession, the upper eyelid will be pushed superiorly giving an eyelid retraction appearance. In summary, vertical muscle recession will widen the palpebral fissure, and resection will narrow the palpebral fissure. BCSC comments that “The superior rectus muscle is loosely bound to the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. The eyelid may be pulled downward following resection of the superior rectus muscle, thus narrowing the palpebral fissure. In contrast, the eyelid is not usually retracted upward with small or moderate recessions.” This is a true fact but here, the recession is large. For a hypertropia of 30 PD, one has to do at least a 10 mm recession (approximately 3 PD = 1mm recession). This is considered a large recession. Hence, one would expect a widening of the palpebral fissure after such a recession.

question: You have a 20-year-old patient with 40 prism diopters of alternating exotropia who has never had strabismus surgery. You wish to perform a recess / resect procedure on the left eye. What would be a reasonable surgical plan based on the Park's criteria?

options.A: Left medial rectus resection 4 mm and left lateral rectus recession 3 mm
options.B: Left medial rectus resection 3 mm and left lateral rectus recession 4 mm
options.C: Left medial rectus resection 8 mm and left lateral rectus recession 6 mm
options.D: Left medial rectus resection 6 mm and left lateral rectus recession 8 mm

explanation: Nobody expects you to memorize the Park's criteria and there is no reason to memorize all the exact correction values unless you plan to be a strabismus surgeon. These types of questions generally test whether you know which muscle needs to be operated on, what type of procedure should be done (recession vs. resection), and whether the procedure requires a large or small intervention. The first step in answering this type of question is deciding what type of procedure need to be performed. We will use lay terms to explain this. In an exotropia the patient will require tightening of the medial rectus (resection) and loosening / weakening of the lateral rectus muscle (recession). All of these answer choices list those options so that was not very helpful for this particular question. Next it is important to know that in correcting any horizontal strabismus (exo or eso deviaton), the lateral rectus will always require more correction than the medial rectus. This is necessary because the lateral rectus is a very long muscle and the dose-response curve is less steep than the short, tight medial rectus. 1 mm of resection or recession of the medial rectus will give much more effect than 1 mm of resection or recession of the lateral rectus. Finally you need to know that for any 15 diopter horizontal strabismus (exo or eso deviation), your correction will be 4 mm on the lateral rectus and 3 mm on the medial rectus; the deviation type will tell you whether to resect or recess. Now you know that the 40 diopter exotropia presented in this question will require much more than a 4 mm medial rectus resection and a 3 mm lateral rectus recession. The only good answer, therefore, is choice D. Use this same logic for similar strabismus questions and you can't go wrong.

question: A 1-year-old child presents with 30-prism diopters of esotropia which has been present for 6 months according to his mother. You find significant upshoot during adduction of either eye. You also examine this child's twin sister who also has 30-prism diopters of esotropia, but no significant upshoot during adduction of either eye. Both children show alternate fixation and negligible refractive errors. What is the best course of management for both children?

options.B: inferior oblique weakening and bilateral medial rectus recessions for the first child; bilateral medial rectus recessions of the same magnitude for the 2nd child
options.C: inferior oblique weakening and bilateral medial rectus recessions for the first child; bilateral medial rectus recessions of greater magnitude for the 2nd child
options.D: inferior oblique weakening and bilateral medial rectus recessions for the first

explanation: Both children have congenital esotropia, but only the first child has inferior oblique overaction (IOOA). Since inferior oblique weakening does not significantly change primary position alignment, you should perform the same level of medial rectus recessions in both cases.

question: Which of the following strabismus surgeries poses the greatest threat to visual acuity of the operated eye if a complication occurs?
explanation: Strengthening of the inferior oblique requires reinsertion more posteriorly which predisposes the macula to greater danger should scleral perforation occur. Comments: Dear editor, I am confused. I thought to strengthen a muscle you resect it, but reinsert it at the same position as before. If the muscle is reinserted more posteriorly, then it should become weaker. Is that incorrect? "strengthening" a muscle can be achieved by either method. Inserting the IO more posteriorly effectively enhances its primary action (elevating). Review the anatomy and you'll see it makes senses. the IO and SO kind of act in reverse bc of their pully like system To answer the first suggestion - as I understand, you can reinsert to the same location for smaller adjustments, but can insert at a more "distal" location for larger adjustment as well. To answer why tighter = posteriorly, the oblique muscles' functional origins are ANTERIOR to its insertion on the globe. The distal direction of both insertions is more posteriorly - it's easier to take this in looking at a model (or at least a picture). Why is it called "advancement" when you reinsert the muscle posteriorly ??? Bc you advance the muscle in the vector with which it was inserted. Ie posterior temporally and superiorly for the IO

question: A 22-year-old man presents to your office for a 3rd opinion regarding possible strabismus surgery. He is self-conscious about the appearance of his eyes, with his left eye being constantly elevated. He states that he has had this problem with his eyes since birth. His twin sister has a similar problem. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: One key distinguishing feature between congenital fibrosis syndrome and thyroid eye disease is the former's congenital origin. There are several variations of congenital fibrosis syndrome and they can present in both sporadic and inherited patterns. One variation, "vertical retraction syndrome," affects the superior rectus such that the patient cannot depress his eye.

question: Which of the following is the most often used procedure in the treatment of type 1 Duane's syndrome with a significant face turn?

options.A: lateral rectus resection on the involved side
options.B: medial rectus recession on the involved side
options.C: lateral rectus resection on the uninvolved side
options.D: medial rectus recession on the uninvolved side

explanation: The most common surgical management of type 1 Duane's syndrome is medial rectus recession on the involved side. If the deviation is greater than 20 prism diopters, then bilateral medial rectus recessions are often performed. Most strabismologists would not perform lateral rectus resection due to the risk of worsening globe retraction. One of the memory tools that is often used to remember the different types of Duane's syndrome is: Type 1 - one "D" - abDuction deficit (thus esotropia) Type 2 - two "D"s) - aDDuction deficit (thus exotropia) Type 3 - three "D"s): abDuction and aDDuction deficit For Duane syndrome, instead of type 1-3, there is a shift into calling them esotropic Duane, exotropic Duane, and orthotropic Duane. Duane retraction syndrome is a spectrum of innervation anomalies where there is a congenital misinnervation of the lateral rectus muscle. In addition to variable amounts of limitation of abduction or adduction, there is also concurrent contraction of the medial and lateral muscles on attempted adduction. The tethering effect of the tight lateral rectus causes the overshoots in adduction. Surgical intervention is taken when there is a anomalous head position, and sometimes to treat the overshoots and globe retraction. The first procedure for esotropic Duane's (Type 1) is medial rectus recession. Recently, superior rectus recession combined with medial rectus recession have shown to provide good outcomes. In patients with exotropia Duane's (Type 2), the classic teaching is lateral rectus recession. Exotropic Duane with overshoot may be managed with Y-splitting of the lateral rectus muscle. If there is concurrent globe retraction, then the recession includes the medial rectus muscle as well (i.e. recession of anatagonist co-contracting muscle). Comments: What about type 3 Duane? In the 2020-2021 Peds BCSC, Chapter 12 (pg. 134), they do not require surgical treatment if they have minimal head turn or horizontal strabismus. Surgery can be considered if there's severe globe retraction, in which recession of both the MR and LR can be done. There are also other procedures that I will leave to the book to describe (I don't know them well).

question: You are examining a child who is brought in by his mother for a recent history of "eye drifts upward." There is a left hypertropia, most obvious on right gaze. On alternate cover testing, you notice refixation downward of the left eye when it is uncovered. In addition, there is an upward shift of the right eye when the left eye is covered on alternate cover testing. Which of the following best explains this child's ocular deviation?
explanation: This patient demonstrates a left hypertropia when the left eye is adducting. In addition, there is a refixation movement downward for the left eye on alternate cover testing (and upward for the right eye) which demonstrates that Hering's law of equal innervation is being obeyed. This is consistent with a diagnosis of left inferior oblique overaction. If no refixation movement of the higher eye was found, this would be more consistent with dissociated vertical deviation which does not obey Hering's law. Comments: DVD and IOOA both cause a hypertropia. The question starts by saying a left hypertropia, so there is no way this could be a right DVD or IOOA, so C and D are out. DVD is the outward and upward drift of an eye when it is not fixing: in some cases because of intermittent suppression, when testing because it is covered. DVD violates Hering's law and is dissociated, by definition, meaning that when the eye with DVD has a refixation movement, the other eye should not move at all (left hyper, alternate cover: cover moving right to left should cause the left eye to drift up from now being suppressed under the cover; cover moving left to right should give left downward refixation with right eye staying still). IOOA, on the other hand, will give bilateral refixation movements (left hyper, alternate cover: cover moving right to left should give bilateral upwards refixation, cover moving left to right should give bilateral downward refixation). The key to the question is the right eye moving down during right cover. This does not happen in DVD, only in true left hypertropia, such as IOOA.

question: You are examining a patient who displays poor elevation of the right eye in adduction. Forced duction testing is positive for a restriction, but you are unsure whether this represents an inferior rectus restriction versus a Brown syndrome. Which of the following maneuvers would help distinguish a Brown syndrome from an inferior rectus restriction?
explanation: Both inferior rectus restriction and Brown syndrome will present with deficient elevation on adduction. To accentuate the restriction in Brown syndrome, elevation in adduction can be tested during forced duction test. In forced duction test, to test the oblique muscle, you retropulse the globe with forceps; to test the rectus muscle, you proptose globe with your forceps. Retropulsion stretches the superior oblique tendon and therefore, the restriction would be increased if it is due to Brown syndrome. In contrast for inferior rectus restriction, the restriction would be increased during forceps-induced proptosis (i.e. not retropulsion). For forced ductions of the rectus muscles, one performs the movement in the opposite direction of the suspected restriction. If you are elevating the eye with the forceps, you are checking restrictions of the inferior rectus. If you are depressing the eye, you are checking restrictions of the superior rectus. If you are abducting the eye, you are checking restriction of the medial rectus. Lastly, if you are adducting the eye, you are checking restriction of the lateral rectus. For forced ductions of the oblique muscles, the purpose of the test is to grade the over- or under-action of the inferior or superior oblique muscles. When you intort the eye, you are grading the inferior oblique. When you extort the eye, you are grading the superior oblique. For those training in programs where you perform Guyton's exaggerated traction test as forced ductions for the oblique muscles, what I am describing here is different. Guyton's exaggerated traction test checks the inferior oblique muscle with the eyeball in the adducted and elevated, retropulsed position. One performs a temporal sweeping move and the significance of the "bump" felt underneath is the grade of the inferior oblique. Similarly for the superior oblique, one checks the eyeball in the adducted and depressed retropulsed position. Then, one performs a temporal sweeping move to feel the "bump" for the grade of the superior oblique. NYSTAGMUS/DIPLOPIA

question: A 14-year-old girl presents to your clinic with a 3-month history of peculiar eye movements. On exam, you note pendular elevation and intorsion of one eye while simultaneously, the other eye displays pendular depression and extorsion. What lesion is most commonly responsible for this eye movement disorder in children?
explanation: The clinical vignette describes the entity of see-saw nystagmus where you can imagine one eye is "going up" while the other eye is "going down" just like the playground device. This type of nystagmus is typically caused by a lesion in the parasellar or midbrain area. In children, the most common responsible lesion is a craniopharyngioma which may also cause bitemporal hemianopia visual field defects. The treatment for see-saw nystagmus is removal of the responsible lesion. Also, baclofen and clonazepam may help dampen this nystagmus. Here is a list of the commonly-tested nystagmus or nystagmoid patterns and the responsible lesions/locations: Downbeat -- cervicomedullary junction (e.g. Chiari type 1 malformation), cerebellar flocculus See-saw -- parasellar area (e.g. craniopharyngioma), midbrain Opsoclonus -- neuroblastoma [usually from adrenals] Periodic alternating nystagmus -- cervicomedullary junction, cerebellar nodulus Upbeat -- cerebellum, medulla, midbrain Comments: Think of the pituitary as the fulcrum of the see saw

question: You are examining a 4-year-old child who has a history of congenital esotropia, but who never underwent strabismus surgery. Curiously, he can read the 20/25 line with both eyes open, but only the 20/60 line with either eye occluded. You also notice that he displays horizontal jerk nystagmus and alternating head movements when either eye is occluded. There is no nystagmus when there is no occlusion. What is the characteristic waveform of this child's nystagmus and which way does he turn his head when his right eye is occluded?

options.A: exponential INCREASE in slow phase velocity; turn head to the RIGHT
options.B: exponential INCREASE in slow phase velocity; turn head to the LEFT
options.C: exponential DECREASE in slow phase velocity; turn head to the RIGHT
options.D: exponential DECREASE in slow phase velocity; turn head to the LEFT

explanation: This child displays horizontal jerk nystagmus only when either eye is occluded. In addition, his visual acuity is good with both eyes open, but worsens when either eye is covered. These features are classic for latent nystagmus. Latent nystagmus is more common in children with congenital esotropia and dissociated vertical deviation and is usually diagnosed in early childhood. Since vision is markedly reduced under monocular testing conditions, these children should not be completely occluded in either eye when assessing visual acuity. Instead, the eye not being tested can be fogged with a +5.00 lens or the occluder can be held several inches away from the non-tested eye. The characteristic waveform in latent nystagmus is an exponential DECREASE in the slow phase velocity. This pattern is opposite that of congenital motor nystagmus which shows an exponential INCREASE in the slow phase velocity. In latent nystagmus, the fast phase is toward the eye that is NOT occluded. Therefore, there will be a right jerk nystagmus when the left eye is occluded and a left jerk nystagmus when the right eye is occluded. For this child, to take advantage of the null point, the child will want to look toward the RIGHT (i.e. adduction of the left eye) when the right eye is occluded since a left jerk nystagmus will be present. To achieve this, the child will turn his head to the LEFT.

question: A 13-year-old teenage boy presents to your office with worsening abnormal eye movements that his parents have noticed over the past 6 months. In primary gaze, the boy displays a jerk nystagmus with the fast component beating downward. He appears to be adopting a chin-down head position to dampen this nystagmus. The rest of his ocular exam is normal. Which of the following choices is the most likely underlying cause of this teenager's nystagmus?
explanation: This teenager is displaying a jerk nystagmus in primary gaze, with the fast phase beating in a downward direction. This is the definition of downbeat nystagmus which is most often caused by an Arnold-Chiari malformation. An Arnold-Chiari malformation basically consists of a defect of the base of the skull and the upper spinal area. These defects may lead to downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum (the opening at the base of the skull). There are several types of Arnold-Chiari malformations, discussion of which is beyond the scope of this website. Here is a list of the commonly-tested nystagmus or nystagmoid patterns and the responsible lesions/locations: Spasmus nutans -- usually no tumor; but similar nystagmus with parasellar/hypothalamic tumors Downbeat -- cervicomedullary junction (e.g. Arnold-Chiari malformation), cerebellar flocculus See-saw -- parasellar area (e.g. craniopharyngioma), midbrain Opsoclonus -- neuroblastoma [usually from adrenals] Periodic alternating nystagmus -- cervicomedullary junction, cerebellar nodulus Upbeat -- cerebellum, medulla, midbrain

question: A 4-year-old child with a history of congenital nystagmus presents to your office as a referral from his pediatrician. The mother of the child wants something non-invasive to be done for the child's abnormal head turn. On examination, you note that the child adopts a large left head turn to dampen his left jerk nystagmus. How would you orient Fresnel prisms over each eye to help reduce this child's left head turn?

options.A: base-in prism over right eye; base-in prism over left eye
options.B: base-out prism over right eye; base-in prism over left eye
options.C: base-out prism over right eye; base-out prism over left eye
options.D: base-in prism over right eye; base-out prism over left eye

explanation: To reduce significant head turns in children with nystagmus, you orient the prisms so their apices are pointing toward the null zone. This effectively shifts the image into the null zone. For this child, his null zone is in right gaze. Therefore, the prism over the right eye should be base-in while the prism over the left eye should be base-out. For surgical correction of a head turn due to nystagmus, strabismus surgery is performed to rotate the eyes away from the null point.

question: You diagnose a 3-year-old child with congenital motor nystagmus (CMN). He displays a left jerk nystagmus and an abnormal head posture. What would be this child's expected head posture?
explanation: By convention, the fast-beating component defines the direction of the nystagmus. Thus, a "left jerk nystagmus" indicates that the fast component is left-beating. "Alexander's law" states that the nystagmus is more pronounced when gaze is directed toward the side of the fast-beating component. In this case, there is a left jerk nystagmus; thus it would worsen in left gaze and improve on right gaze. To improve visual acuity, most children with CMN would adopt a head/face turn that would minimize the nystagmus movements. For this scenario since the nystagmus dampens on right gaze, the child would adopt a left head turn.

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with new-onset, binocular double vision for the past few weeks. She states that these symptoms have never happened before. Her external photograph is shown above. The patient is bothered by the diplopia and wants something done about it. She exhibits significant right hypotropia with severe restriction of elevation of the right eye. What represents the best course of management for the most common cause of this condition at this time point?
explanation: The external photograph depicts significant upper eyelid retraction. Therefore, this patient has new-onset diplopia from thyroid eye disease until proven otherwise. Typically, stability of the deviation for at least 6 months should be demonstrated before any strabismus surgery is performed. Also as stressed repeatedly on board examinations, the proper order of surgery for thyroid eye disease patients is: (1) orbital decompression (if significant proptosis is present); (2) strabismus surgery (for significant/symptomatic deviations); and then (3) eyelid surgery (e.g. lowering of upper eyelids to decrease exposure symptoms).

question: A perplexed father brings in his 3-year-old son who is exhibiting abnormal eye and head movements since early infancy. On exam, the child appears to have a right jerk nystagmus that remains horizontal even in vertical gaze. You step out for a moment to answer a message, and when you return, you are surprised to see that the child now displays a left jerk nystagmus. Given the likely diagnosis, approximately how long was your telephone call?
explanation: The clinical vignette is alluding to the rare entity of periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) which may occur in congenital or acquired forms. In both forms, the jerk nystagmus lasts for approximately 60-90 seconds in one direction. There is then a period of no nystagmus for 10-20 seconds and then a resumption of jerk nystagmus in the opposite direction. The child with PAN may demonstrate alternating head turning to take advantage of the shifting null point (e.g. right head turn [i.e. left gaze] during the right jerk phase). Though the cause of PAN is currently unknown, it is thought to be due to a state of vestibular overactivity. Congenital PAN also has been associated with oculocutaneous albinism.1 The acquired form of PAN is usually associated with a lesion of the cervicomedullary junction (e.g. cerebellar nodulus or uvula). Other causes of acquired PAN include: multiple sclerosis, Chiari I malformation, and cerebellar degenerations

question: A 10-year-old boy presents to your office with a several month history of "restricted eye movements" as related by his mother. His Snellen visual acuity is 20/25 OU. His pupil exam is significant for being poorly reactive to light, but more reactive to near testing. His motility exam shows poor upgaze saccades with his eyes appearing to "sink in" when attempting upgaze. Which of the following is likely the underlying cause of this child's ocular condition?
explanation: This child displays the classic ocular signs of dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka "Parinaud syndrome"). These signs include: paralysis of upgaze defective (voluntary) convergence pupillary light-near dissociation convergence-retraction "nystagmus" eyelid retraction ("Collier's sign") The convergence-retraction "nystagmus" is not considered a true nystagmus but rather a disjunctive saccadic oscillation. To elicit this movement, the patient is asked to track a downward-rotating OKN drum which will elicit an attempted upward saccade. Instead of a normal upward saccade, the patient with this syndrome will exhibit convergence and retraction of both eyes since there is co-contraction of all horizontal extraocular muscles (the medial recti acting more forcefully than the lateral recti). However, voluntary convergence movements are minimal. Typically, upward saccades are initially affected but upward pursuit movements can become affected as well. Eventually, even vestibulo-ocular responses (i.e. Dolls' head responses) and Bell's phenomenon can be paralyzed. In children, the most common causes of dorsal midbrain syndrome are pinealoma and congenital aqueductal stenosis. In young adult women, it is typically caused by multiple sclerosis. In elderly patients, the most common cause is midbrain stroke.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with new-onset double vision for the past week. You notice an overshoot of the upper eyelids when the eyes return to primary gaze after prolonged downgaze. Which of the following would confirm your putative diagnosis for this patient?

options.A: MRI/MRA of the brain with specific attention to the Circle of Willis

explanation: The overshoot described is also known as a "Cogan lid twitch" and is classic for ocular myasthenia gravis. Other ancillary tests to diagnose myasthenia gravis include the classic Tensilon test (or Prostigmin test), the "ice-pack" test, the "sleep test", autoantibody tests (e.g. anti-MuSK, anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies), and single-fiber electromyography.

question: A 3-year-old child with a history of congenital nystagmus presents to your office as a referral from his pediatrician. The mother wants something to be done for the child's abnormal head turn. On examination, you note that the child adopts a large left head turn to dampen his left jerk nystagmus. The child has already tried prism therapy, but was not compliant with keeping the glasses on. Which of the following strabismus surgeries could help reduce this child's head turn?

options.A: recession of the right lateral and left medial rectus muscles; resection of the right medial and left lateral rectus muscles
options.B: recession of the right medial and left lateral rectus muscles; resection of the left medial and right lateral rectus muscles
options.C: recession of both lateral rectus muscles; resection of both medial rectus muscles
options.D: recession of all the horizontal rectus muscles to a position anterior to the

explanation: This question basically asks you to describe the Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure which shifts the null point closer to primary position. In this surgery, the eyes are rotated toward the head turn or away from the null point. Thus, for a left head turn, the eyes are surgically rotated to the left. To achieve this, recessions of the left medial and right lateral recti and resections of the left lateral and right medial recti are performed. An alternative to the Kestenbaum procedure is recession of all the horizontal rectus muscles to a position posterior (not anterior) to the equator. In contrast, to achieve this effect with prisms, the apices of the prisms are directed toward the null zone. Comments: One way to think of this is you are doing an "Eso-Exo" procedure to correct the head turn. One eye is exotropic (in this case the right) and the other is Esotropic (the left in this question). Then simply do an esotropia surgery (LMR recess, LLR Resect) on the left eye and an exotropia surgery on the right (RLR Recess, RMR Resect) why do you surgically shift the eye AWAY form the null point? The best way I can think of it is: You are simply moving the null point from a right gaze to straight ahead. The muscles still "think" they are in that right gaze preference, but now they eyes are straight because you moved the muscles. -That's not a perfect explanation, but it works for my brain. Just to clarify: for a non-surgical therapy, base left prisms would be prescribed. Is this correct? Yes, exactly. You are essentially trying to allow the patient to remain in the "null" gaze (in this case, right gaze) with base left prism, without needing to head-tilt left. You are treating the head tilt in essence.

question: You are evaluating a 4-year-old child referred by her pediatrician for abnormal eye movements. Unfortunately, the caretakers of the child cannot provide any birth or other relevant history since they just adopted the child. On exam, the child exhibits a horizontal right-beating nystagmus. There is no abnormal head posture. The child has 20/25 visual acuity OU on Snellen testing and no afferent pupillary defect OU. His cycloplegic refraction is +2.00 sphere OU and his fundus exam is normal. Which of the following would be most specific to confirm the child's most likely diagnosis?

options.A: determining if the nystagmus is purely uniplanar
options.B: recording the nystagmus waveform to determine if there is any pendular component
options.C: looking for increased amplitude of the nystagmus while rotating an OKN drum to the child's left
options.D: looking for decreased amplitude of the nystagmus while rotating an OKN

explanation: Based on the child's clinical findings of a horizontal nystagmus with good vision, the most likely/common diagnosis is congenital motor nystagmus (CMN). Though CMN is typically horizontal on upgaze and downgaze (i.e. uniplanar), absence of this feature does not preclude a diagnosis of CMN. Also, other nystagmus entities, like congenital sensory nystagmus, can present with a horizontal, uniplanar pattern. Similarly, CMN can present with other patterns besides the more common jerk nystagmus. These patterns include pendular, circular, or elliptical. One feature that occurs ONLY in CMN is "paradoxical inversion of the OKN response." In other forms of jerk nystagmus, if a child with right jerk nystagmus views an OKN drum rotating to the left (thus stimulating pursuit left and jerk right), his nystagmus would increase in amplitude. However in a child with CMN, his right jerk nystagmus would actually dampen or even reverse to become a left jerk nystagmus. This peculiar phenomenon ONLY occurs in congenital motor nystagmus.

question: A 1-year-old baby boy presents to your clinic after his mother had noticed persistent abnormal head movements for the past few months. On exam, the child appears to be nodding his head at a rate of 2 Hz. His vision is CuSM OU, there is no afferent pupillary defect, he is orthotropic, and his dilated fundus exam is normal. You also notice a very fine, high-frequency horizontal nystagmus affecting the right eye more than the left eye. Which of the following would also be expected given the child's most likely diagnosis?

options.A: alternating nystagmus with either eye occluded
options.D: persistence of nystagmus till approximately age 12-18 years

explanation: This child presents with an asymmetric, low-amplitude, high-frequency nystagmus with head nodding. This nystagmus has also been described as "shimmering". These features are consistent with spasmus nutans. The clinical triad of spasmus nutans is: (1) head nodding; (2) monocular or asymmetric nystagmus; and (3) torticollis (i.e. abnormal or stiff neck position). Spasmus nutans typically presents in children between 4 and 14 months of age. The direction of the nystagmus is typically horizontal, but it can also be vertical or rotary. It is typically of the pendular variety. Spasmus nutans per se is a benign entity that typically resolves by 5 years of age (the BCSC says by 3-4 years of age). However, tumors of the parasellar/hypothalamic area can present with a nearly indistinguishable nystagmus; thus many authorities will perform neuroimaging in all cases of spasmus nutans (controversial topic). Lastly, a nystagmus resembling spasmus nutans can occur in children with certain retinal disorders, like congenital stationary night blindness or rod/rod-cone dystrophy. Thus, further testing (e.g. electroretinogram) is warranted if the child displays other ocular abnormalities (e.g. abnormal fundus exam, paradoxical pupils, etc). Some extra info from Pediatric Ophthalmologist extraordinaire, Dr. Charlotte Gore: CSM ("central, steady, and maintained") describes fixation on a target. "C" and "S" are monocular checks (i.e. one eye covered) while "M" is a binocular check: "C" -- if the tested eye fixates centrally "nC" -- if the tested eye fixates eccentrically "S" -- if the tested eye keeps steady fixation on the target "uS" -- if the tested eye wanders or searches for the target "M" -- in a cover-uncover test, if the original uncovered eye maintains fixation as the occluder is removed from the covered eye "uM" -- in a cover-uncover test, if the previously-covered eye picks up fixation as it is uncovered nC suggest congenital retinal disease or a blind eye uS suggests nystagmus uM suggests amblyopia (i.e. one eye has preferred fixation) Comments: Spas"mus" ("mus"t do an MRI) NoTANs ("No"dding, "T"orticollis, "A"ssymetric "N"ystamgu"s")

question: A child with a history of congenital nystagmus and long-standing right head turn presents to you for surgical management. You decide you will perform the Kestenbaum procedure for this child. You write down the proposed amounts of recession/resection for each of the muscles as follows: RMRRec - 7.0 mm LMRRes - 8.4 mm LLRRec - 9.8 mm RLRRes - ? Unfortunately, you cannot read your handwriting for the amount of the right lateral rectus resection. What is the value of "?" for this child?
explanation: The rationale of the Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure for correcting head turns associated with nystagmus is to shift the null zone closer to primary position. To achieve this, one surgically rotates the eye toward the head turn or away from the null zone. In this case for a right head turn, the eyes are surgically rotated to the right by performing resections of the right lateral and left medial recti and recessions of the right medial and left lateral recti. The total amount of surgery for each eye is equal to ensure that the eyes are rotated an equal amount. For this child, the total amount of surgery planned for his left eye is 8.4 + 9.8 mm = 18.2 mm. Thus, the amount of right lateral rectus resection must be 18.2 - 7.0 = 11.2 mm. Comments: Isnt that exceeding the maximum amount of resection on lateral rectus? Is this accurate? Lateral rectus procedures result in greater changes to eye position due to longer arc of contact. It seems to me that just "adding medial and lateral corrections" is a bit easy.

question: Which of the following is the best way to elicit the "convergence- retraction nystagmus" of a patient with dorsal midbrain syndrome?

options.A: have the patient track an object which is being moved AWAY from him or her
options.B: have the patient track an object which is being moved TOWARD him or her
options.C: have the patient track an upward-rotating OKN drum
options.D: have the patient track a downward-rotating OKN drum

explanation: The classic signs of dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka "Parinaud syndrome") are: paralysis of upgaze defective (voluntary) convergence pupillary light-near dissociation convergence-retraction "nystagmus" eyelid retraction ("Collier's sign") The convergence-retraction "nystagmus" is not considered a true nystagmus but rather a disjunctive saccadic oscillation. To elicit this movement, the patient is asked to track a downward-rotating OKN drum which will elicit an attempted upward saccade. Instead of a normal upward saccade, the patient with this syndrome will exhibit convergence and retraction of both eyes since there is co-contraction of all horizontal extraocular muscles (the medial recti acting more forcefully than the lateral recti). However, voluntary convergence movements are minimal. Typically, upward saccades are initially affected but upward pursuit movements can become affected as well. Eventually, even vestibulo-ocular responses (i.e. Dolls' head responses) and Bell's phenomenon can be paralyzed. In children, the most common causes of dorsal midbrain syndrome are pinealoma and congenital aqueductal stenosis. In young adult women, it is typically caused by multiple sclerosis. In elderly patients, the most common cause is midbrain stroke.

question: An 11-year-old girl is referred to your clinic for a history of long-standing nystagmus. On examination, you note a right jerk nystagmus that worsens in right gaze, but improves on left gaze. Which of the following laws does this nystagmus obey?
explanation: "Alexander's law" states that the nystagmus is more pronounced when gaze is directed toward the side of the fast-beating component. In this case, there is a right jerk nystagmus, thus it worsens in right gaze and improves on left gaze. There is no such thing as "Listing's law" in Ophthalmology. However, there is something called "Listing's plane" which contains the center of rotation of the eye and includes its x and z axes (see "Motor Physiology" chapter in the Peds BCSC book). "Donder's law" states that every tertiary eye position is associated with a specific torsional rotation. "Sherrington's law of reciprocal innervation" states that contraction of a given muscle (e.g. medial rectus) is accompanied by a decrease in contraction of its antagonist (e.g. lateral rectus). This law is violated by Duane's syndrome where co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti can occur. "Hering's law of equal innervation" states that yoke muscles receive equal innervational input when they are activated. For example, when looking straight up, both superior rectus muscles receive the same magnitude of innervational input. This law is violated by the condition of dissociated vertical deviation (DVD). CORNEAL ABNORMALITIES

question: You are examining a child who presents with corneal clouding of both eyes. Which of the following findings would most strongly rule-in a diagnosis of congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) versus congenital hereditary stromal dystrophy (CHSD)?
explanation: Both CHED and CHSD are potential causes of congenital corneal opacity. Since CHSD is extremely rare (e.g. only a few families have been reported in the literature), it is typically not remembered in the "S-T-U-M-P-E-D" mnemonic for different causes of congenital corneal opacity: Sclerocornea Trauma Ulcer Mucopolysaccharidoses Peters anomaly Endothelial (e.g. CHED) Dermoid Basically, the most salient difference between CHED and CHSD is that there is no edema in CHSD (and especially no epithelial edema), though the thickness may be slightly increased in CHSD compared to normal infants. CHSD is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by "flaky" opacities throughout the stroma. CHSD is painless and not associated with either tearing or photophobia. In CHSD and CHED, intraocular pressure and horizontal corneal diameters are normal. This helps to distinguish CHSD and CHED from congenital glaucoma. There used to be a CHED 1 and CHED 2 classification, but recent genetic studies have reclassified CHED type 1 as the same entity as Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPMD), as both are autosomal dominant on the same locus at pericentromeric chromosome 20. CHED type 2 is now reclassified as just CHED, and is autosomal recessive (BCSC Peds and Cornea 2017-2018).

question: What is the most common location of limbal dermoids?
explanation: A common associated syndrome of limbal dermoids is Goldenhar syndrome (aka "oculoauriculovertebral syndrome") whose other manifestations include hemifacial microsomia, ear deformities (including preauricular appendages), upper eyelid colobomas, and vertebral anomalies. A great way to remember this is that the inferotemporal limbus is closest to the ear lobe which itself is frequently involved in Goldenhar syndrome.

question: Which of the following is the major reason for long-term vision loss in infants with tears in Descemet's membrane caused by forceps injury?
explanation: Disruption of Descemet's membrane from forceps injury can result in stromal and epithelial corneal edema. However, this edema usually clears relatively quickly. This disruption can result in anisometropic astigmatism which commonly can cause long- term vision loss from amblyopia.

question: Which of the following features is MOST likely to be associated with megalocornea?

options.C: requires gonioscopy to be able to see the anterior chamber angle
options.D: carrier mothers have slightly enlarged corneal diameters

explanation: Megalocornea is a X-linked condition. Carrier mothers often have slightly enlarged corneal diameters. 90% of affected patients are male. The condition is usually not associated with increased intraocular pressure and must be differentiated from infantile glaucoma. Megalocornea is usually an isolated finding and is not progressive. It may be associated with lens subluxation, iris hypoplasia, radial iris transillumination defects, and ectopic pupil. Oftentimes, the anterior chamber angle can be seen directly without the need for gonioscopy. Comments: Mega = Large or size XL. The inheritance of megalocornea is X-Linked (XL). Therefore, MEGAlocornea = XL (a large sized cornea and X-Linked)

question: You are managing an 18-year-old patient with the ocular abnormalities shown in the photographs above. This patient is also taking a prostaglandin analog for glaucoma in both eyes. Mutations in which of the following genes is most likely to be responsible for this patient's ocular condition?
explanation: The photographs demonstrate the classic ocular findings of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome (ARS): (1) posterior embryotoxon; (2) iris strands; and (3) corectopia with possible hole formation. ARS is typically an autosomal dominant disorder with mutations in the PITX2 and FOXC1 genes demonstrated to cause this phenotype. (Image credit: Cogan Pathology Collection found at: http://cogancollection.nei.nih.gov). Comments: TIGR/MYOC = Juvenile OAG, OPTN = Normal Tension Glaucoma, OPA1 = Dominant Optic Atrophy Axe the Foxy (FOXC) Pix(pics) (PITX): Axe for Axenfeld, FOXC1 for first word, PITX2 for second word

question: You are examining a 2-year-old child in the hospital who was admitted for jaundice. Your examination is notable for the anterior segment finding seen in the photograph above. The child's past medical history is also significant for pulmonary stenosis and developmental delay. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this infant?
explanation: The slit-lamp photograph shows posterior embryotoxon which is defined as a thickened, "prominent" Schwalbe line. It is seen in up to 15% of normal patients. I t is a characteristic finding in a variety of syndromes, most commonly Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. This child has jaundice, cardiac defects, and posterior embryotoxon which are characteristic findings of Alagille syndrome (AS). AS is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations of the JAG1 gene on chromosome 20p12. It typically involves the liver, heart, skeleton, and the eye. Other characteristic findings include a broaden forehead, pointed chin, butterfly hemivertebrae, and mild developmental delay. The corneal finding in Wilson's disease is a Kayser-Fleischer ring (not posterior embryotoxon). Comments: - Alagille is also known as Arteriohepatic dysplasia. In addition to posterior embryotoxon, it is also associated with myopia and a pigmentary retinopathy (there is a question about it in the Retina section).

question: What is the generally-accepted measurement cutoff that defines a newborn as having "microcornea"?

options.A: horizontal corneal diameter less than 7 mm
options.B: horizontal corneal diameter less than 9 mm
options.C: horizontal corneal diameter less than 10 mm
options.D: horizontal corneal diameter less than 11 mm

explanation: Microcornea (defined as corneal diameter less than 9 mm in the newborn and less than 10 mm at 2 years of age) can occur in a variety of other ocular conditions including PHPV, colobomas, and nanophthalmos. Microcornea is a condition characterized by a clear cornea of normal thickness, but whose horizontal diameter is less than 10 mm. Individuals with microcornea are typically hyperopic because their corneas are relatively flat. Because of this flat corneal curvature, these individuals are more prone to angle closure glaucoma. For those patients without angle closure glaucoma, still 20% (not 5%) of them will develop an open-angle glaucoma. GLAUCOMA

question: A 2-month-old child is brought to your office because his mother has noticed that his eyes "look bigger than normal." On handlight exam, you notice similar findings for both eyes as seen in the photo above. The horizontal diameters of both corneas measure 13.5 mm. His irises are present and completely normal. On further questioning, the child's mother states that one of her siblings suffered from a similar ocular condition. Mutations in which of the following genes is most likely responsible for this child's condition?
explanation: This photograph depicts diffuse corneal edema as seen by the irregular corneal light reflex. In addition, you are told that the horizontal corneal diameters are 13.5 mm OU which are grossly abnormal (normal in newborn is 9.5-10.5 mm; normal in 1-year-old child is 10.0-11.5 mm). According to the BCSC, glaucoma should be suspected in any child whose corneal diameter is greater than 13.0 mm. Therefore, this child has congenital glaucoma until proven otherwise and should undergo an urgent examination under anesthesia with likely surgical intervention. Though primary congenital glaucoma typically occurs sporadically, it has been associated with gene mutations in certain families. The first gene demonstrated to be involved in congenital glaucoma was CYP1B1 which encodes a protein in the cytochrome P450 enzyme family. Other causative mutations involve the GLC3A, GLC3B and GLC3C genes. You should memorize some of the other glaucomas' gene associations: Axenfeld-Rieger: PITX2 or FOXC1 Juvenile-onset glaucoma: GLC1A (aka MYOC) Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma: LOXL1 Normal tension glaucoma: OPTN

question: An 11-month-old child with a history of primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is brought in by his mother for a 2nd opinion regarding his management. His mother is frustrated because the child has already undergone one goniotomy by a prominent glaucoma specialist, but his intraocular pressure is still in the 30 mmHg range OU. Which of the following options is the next best step for this child?
explanation: Typically, most pediatric glaucoma specialists would attempt a second angle glaucoma surgery (e.g. another goniotomy or trabeculotomy) before moving on to trabeculectomy (+/- MMC) or a glaucoma drainage implant. The success rate of 1 or 2 angle surgeries for PCG in infants presenting from 3 months to 1 year is approximately 80%.

question: A 6-month-old child is referred to your clinic for chronic tearing and "wincing" OU that his mother has noticed since 1 month of age. His ocular exam is seen above. Which of the following ancillary tests is best at monitoring his response to treatment?
explanation: The photograph demonstrates the presence of corneal edema as can be seen by the irregular corneal light reflex. In a child, the primary diagnosis that should be ruled in/out is congenital glaucoma. The classic triad of symptoms for congenital glaucoma are bleparospasm, photophobia, and epiphora (i.e. tearing). This child deserves a full ophthalmic exam, most likely under anesthesia. Of the answer choices above, A-scan ultrasound is the most appropriate ancillary test to monitor disease progression. If one eye is growing excessively compared to the fellow eye, this may indicate poor IOP control in that eye. Remember, congenital glaucoma is primarily managed with surgery, not chronic medical treatment.

question: A 10-year-old child with a history of poorly-controlled juvenile open angle glaucoma presents to your office with intraocular pressures (IOPs) of 26 and 29 mmHg in the right and left eyes respectively. He has a history of Ahmed glaucoma drainage implants in both eyes. He is currently also taking daily methazolamide to help control his IOPs. Which of the following topical glaucoma medications would be LEAST effective given this patient's history?
explanation: This child is already taking a systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (CAI); therefore use of a topical CAI like brinzolamide (brand name: Azopt) would be ineffective. If topical glaucoma medications are indicated for a child (e.g. added control after multiple glaucoma surgical procedures), most specialists would choose the prostaglandin analogs given their lack of systemic side effects. As emphasized repeatedly on this website, the a2-adrenergic agonist, brimonidine (brand name: Alphagan), is contraindicated in children younger than 2 years old. In this age group, brimonidine can cause lethargy, hypotonia, and CNS depression. This medication should also be used with caution in older children. Comments: I don't disagree with the topical CAI while on a current oral CAI, but what about a tube shunt helping outflow and adding a prostaglandin analog to help with trabecular outflow? It seems that the tube will greatly diminish the effect of the latanoprost. And since the other 3 choices offered all work on aqueous production, this would seem to be most likely to help before the latanoprost. Latanoprost works in the uveoescleral outflow, not trabecular True, but the fact that there is a tube in place with high IOP says to me that no outflow is working well so wouldn’t aqueous suppression be more efficacious? Uveoscleral outflow is not IOP dependant, unlike conventional TM IRIS ABNORMALITIES

question: An 8-year-old boy is referred to your office by his pediatrician for a baseline eye exam. Your slit-lamp exam is significant for the findings seen in the photo above. Which of the following statements is most likely true for this patient?

options.A: His underlying condition also features posterior subcapsular cataracts
options.B: This boy is at higher risk for pilocytic astrocytomas of the optic nerve
options.C: This ocular finding may be associated with spontaneous hyphemas
options.D: His underlying disease is caused by an autosomal recessive genetic disease

explanation: The slit-lamp photo shows multiple iris melanocytic hamartomas otherwise known as Lisch nodules. The presence of these nodules constitutes one of the criteria in the diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The clinical diagnosis of NF1 consists of the patient exhibiting 2 or more of the following criteria: a first-degree relative with NF1 6 or more cafe-au-lait spots 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma axillary/inguinal/or other intertriginous freckling 2 or more Lisch nodules a distinctive osseous lesion (e.g. sphenoid bone dysplasia) optic nerve glioma A "pilocytic astrocytoma" of the optic nerve is equivalent to an optic glioma. On neuro- imaging, optic gliomas often appear as "fusiform" or "sausage- shaped" or "kinked" enlargements of the optic nerve. Answer choice "A" refers to the presence of posterior subcapsular cataracts in neurofibromatosis type 2 (there are no characteristic lens changes in NF1). Answer choice "C" refers to what may occur in juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG). The iris lesions in JXG appear as vascularized yellowish or reddish nodules. Answer choice "D" is incorrect since NF1 is autosomal dominant in inheritance. According to U of Michigan's website on this, over 90% of NF1 patients will have Lisch nodules by the age of 6. NF-1 also associated with myelinated NFL and congenital iris ectropion. NF-2 also associated with cortical wedge cataract.

question: You are examining a patient with the peculiar iris abnormalities shown in the photo above. The patient also has twelve discrete hyperpigmented macules on his back and chest areas. What chromosome contains the genetic locus that is responsible for this patient's likely systemic syndrome?
explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts small, sharply-demarcated excrescences of the anterior iris surface known as Lisch nodules. This patient apparently also has multiple cafe-au- lait spots and thus can be clinically diagnosed as having neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1). As stressed repeatedly in board review books, mutations of a genetic locus on chromosome 17 are responsible for this phakomatoses. This fact can be conveniently remembered by the number of letters in the word "neurofibromatosis." Lisch nodules are hamartomatous growths that typically appear in NF-1 patients between ages 5 and 10 years. These nodules are rarely seen before the age of 3 years, while they are present in nearly 100% of all NF-1 adults. The clinical criteria for a diagnosis of NF-1 are summarized here (need 2 or more criteria): a first-degree relative with NF1 6 or more cafe-au-lait spots 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma axillary/inguinal/or other intertriginous freckling 2 or more Lisch nodules a distinctive osseous lesion (e.g. sphenoid bone dysplasia) optic nerve glioma Lastly, a summary of the other answer choices and their respective syndromes: chromosome 9 -- tuberous sclerosis (also chromosome 16) chromosome 22 -- NF-2 A suggested mnemonic (contributed by Dr. Matthew Weed) to remember the diagnostic critiera for NF-1 is: "CALBORN" (Cafe-au-lait spots, Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, Bony deformity, Optic glioma, Relative affected, Neurofibromas)

question: You are called by your local pediatrician to take a look at one of his patients. The pediatrician is concerned by some "iris abnormalities" that he has noticed. Your examination is significant for multiple hypopigmented areas of the iris of this child's left eye as seen in the photo above (arrow). Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this iris finding? (Please ignore this child's congenital heterochromia)

options.A: It can result in secondary glaucoma and corectopia
options.B: It is associated with optic gliomas and hyperpigmented macules of the skin
options.D: It can be associated with oculodermal melanocytosis

explanation: The photograph depicts multiple hypopigmented spots in the iris which are otherwise known as Brushfield spots. They are focal areas of stromal hyperplasia, surrounded by relative hypoplasia and are more common in patients with lightly pigmented irises. These spots are found in approximately 90% of individuals with Down syndrome (i.e. trisomy 21). The spots themselves have no consequence on visual function. Similar nodules, called Wofflin nodules can occur in normal individuals. Answer choice "A" refers to Cogan-Reese syndrome; choice "B" refers to Lisch nodules in association with neurofibromatosis type 1; and choice "D" refers to iris mammillations.

question: Which retinal lesion is associated with the facial skin abnormality depicted in the photo above?
explanation: The photo shows the typical appearance of adenoma sebaceum which is actually a misnomer since these facial lesions actually do not contain adenomatous or sebaceous structures on histopathological sections. A more modern term given to these facial lesions is a facial angiofibroma.
